Illustration 1: An apparently empty cube.alt: Infographic of a transparent cube of air above green hills, with callouts labeling Nitrogen (78%), Oxygen (21%), Water vapor (varies), Dust, Sea salt, Pollen, and Smoke, plus a note that molecules and particles are vastly enlarged.
Illustration 1: An apparently empty cube.caption: The air that looks empty is a mixture of gases, water vapor, and tiny particles.

Visual Spread 1.2: The Layers of the Atm.alt: Infographic of Earth's atmosphere from the ground to space with an altitude scale in km and mi (compressed above 50 km), a temperature curve on the right, labeled layers (Troposphere, Tropopause, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere), Mount Everest, an airliner, a cumulonimbus anvil, ozone layer, weather balloon, meteors, auroras, the ISS, and an apple-skin scale inset.
Visual Spread 1.2: The Layers of the Atm.caption: Nearly all weather happens in the thin lowest layer. Heights above 50 km are compressed to fit.

Illustration 3: The weight of the air.alt: Infographic showing a vertical column of air molecules packed tightly at sea level (1 kg/cm², 14.7 lb/in²) and thinning upward past 5.5 km (half the air), Mount Everest (8.8 km, about 1/3 pressure), and an airliner (~11 km, about 1/4 pressure), with an inset diver showing water pressure increasing with depth.
Illustration 3: The weight of the air.caption: The weight of air above squeezes the lower atmosphere. Pressure falls as you climb.

Illustration 4: Why warm air rises.alt: Two-panel infographic: on the left, equal-size boxes compare densely packed cold air with spread-out warm air; on the right, arrows and a hot-air balloon trace a convection loop rising from a sunny field, cooling sideways, sinking over shaded woods, and returning near the ground.
Illustration 4: Why warm air rises.caption: Same size, different weight: warm air rises over a sunny field while cooler air sinks over shaded woods.

Illustration 5: Unequal heating.alt: Infographic showing parallel sunbeams hitting Earth straight-on near the equator and at a slant near the poles, with arrows carrying heat poleward, a flashlight inset comparing straight and tilted beams, and four labeled thermometers comparing asphalt, grass, water, and snow.
Illustration 5: Unequal heating.caption: The same sunlight is concentrated near the equator and spread over more ground at higher latitudes.

Illustration 6: The water cycle and its.alt: Infographic from ocean to mountains labeling evaporation (heat going in), moisture traveling inland, condensation inside a growing cloud (latent heat coming out), rain and snow, a river returning water to the sea, and a swimmer inset showing evaporative cooling.
Illustration 6: The water cycle and its.caption: Evaporation takes in heat. When vapor condenses into cloud droplets, it releases that heat into the air.

Illustration 7: From high to low.alt: Infographic comparing High pressure (sinking air, clear skies) on the left and Low pressure (rising air, clouds and rain) on the right, with curved surface wind arrows flowing from High toward Low.
Illustration 7: From high to low.caption: Sinking air tends to bring clear skies; rising air cools and builds clouds.

Visual Spread 1.8: The Weather Machine.alt: Wide continuous landscape infographic tracing the eight numbered steps of the weather machine from uneven sunlight over ocean and field, rising warm air, sinking cool air, surface breeze, cloud formation, condensation releasing heat, rain on the hills, and a river returning to the sea, with a 'Start again tomorrow' sun loop.
Visual Spread 1.8: The Weather Machine.caption: The weather machine: sunlight starts a repeating exchange of heat, air, and water.
